headToHead.voiceNote: Cover the names. Every Liam line is one shape on any topic: an over-formal clause applied to something trivial, then a plea or a self-defeating flourish ('culinary block', 'Someone stop this madness!', 'So disruptive!'). Dash's twelve split across three shapes: the comma-'so' inference chain (fifth platform, cheapest room, present at one), the staccato fragment list (half a jacket, Second. Out of two., rooftop/car park), and the live-test self-correction (sorry tests badly). The fragment lists could be read by Crumb or Pixel; only the self-correction and the readout of a result are Dash's alone, and they are the minority. Dash is identifiable by topic (numbers, posts, conversions) more often than by sentence shape.
headToHead.constructionNote: Dash's best are tighter than the bar: the turn sits on the last two to four words ('Date it whenever.', 'The good sleeve.', 'click rate is lawsuits') and nothing trails. Liam's set has a 27-word ramble (#29) and leans on the narrator. Even on construction at the top end; the bar wins only because our depth below the top dozen collapses.
headToHead.quotableNote: Liam owns two internet-famous lines (180/360, 'consequences of my actions'). Dash has three real clips ('together on the fifth', 'click rate is lawsuits', 'present at one'). Even at the top, but the bar's clips are character statements; ours are good jokes any wisecracker could carry.

genericNote: 142 lines in the bank. 35 are voiceless or stock (anyone in the cast could say them with the name covered: Nav owns the nine-oh-one line, Vex owns 'watching your face' and 'thirty tabs deep', Brock owns 'hands are shaking' and 'clap first', Tilly owns 'keeping the exact wording', and the booth/closer/lose lines are generic sad-sack sincerity). A further 16 are the weakest members of templates that recur five or more times. 51 of 142 = 36%.
templates: Bad fact, 'so', happy wrong conclusion (the persona's spine, now carrying about 30 lines: landslide, fifth platform, present at one, car park rooftop, request it twice, lost forty so due, hear the please, Prince charged me so he likes me, Vex accurate, Brock's cheers worthless, Tilly nicer, underdog so favourite, beat the traffic, no is information, laughs up, late peak, rival got a laugh, rough draft/edit, four minutes so mine's two, Crumb vacancy, Nav recalculate, hum isn't playing, cheapest room, left before it could, top two out of two, watch twice, polite one, both got taste, near as on, nobody checked). ruleBreaks: Word limits: none over. At the cap: openers 'Variant A: you're stunning. Variant B: I'm stunning. I voted. B's ahead.', 'I walked on and nobody booed, so I'm calling tonight a landslide.', 'I rated everyone on the way in, you won, I'm your prize.' (12/12); all ten jabs are 8 to 10 words, seven at exactly 10; 'Tilly can't end a call, which sounds sweet until hour six, and I've done hour six, and it was sweet.' and 'My password is your name, I set it this morning, so if this goes badly I'm locked out of everything.' at 20/20.
No em dashes, no emoji, no asterisks, no stage directions, no real people or brands, nothing beyond PG-13.

Persona rule (one startup word per line, never rename a romance beat in startup words) broken: 'Hi, I'm Dash. Pre-revenue, post-heartbreak, and open to acquisition.' (two terms, renames being single); 'Okay. Pulling the product. Not because of you. Market conditions. You're the market!' (three terms, renames the exit); 'I refresh. Not the page. You. Every eight seconds, checking if you've converted yet.' (converted = said yes); 'Prince, I respect the hustle. But your open rate is zero and your click rate is lawsuits.' (two terms; forgivable, the target is a spam bot).

(the last clause restates the turn); 'Tilly can't end a call, which sounds sweet until hour six, and I've done hour six, and it was sweet.' (double reversal, the button muddies).

That's what I reach for when I'm nervous. I'm always nervous.'; 'Whoever's doing best, which normally I'd say is me, but I'm trying honesty tonight, so not me.'

Stock romance filler: 'Ninety seconds in, you're the most beautiful person I've ever described, and I've described about six.' (most beautiful person); 'My hands are shaking. Good shaking. I didn't know there was a good kind.' (butterflies in other words); 'I like you, and I don't want anyone else to see it.' (plain, and fine as the one dropped-pitch beat, but it is filler).

Tricolon lists: 'Pre-revenue, post-heartbreak, and open to acquisition.'; 'It's cosy, it's private, and it's the only suite where you'd have to stand this close to me.'; 'Late-night radio, completely free, on every night, and honestly, at that price, what are you waiting for?'
Muddy turns (the joke is withheld, not landed): 'Prince charges for compliments, I give mine away, plenty left.'; 'Brock does reps, I do results, he's got more though.'

Warm/cold mismatch: Pixel cold closer 'Honestly, I'd stay till the screen went dark, then a bit longer, in case it's buffering.' is as sincere as the warm one ('Yes. I'd stay, and I wouldn't even post about it.'); the cold beat should sound like a flop, not a second yes.
biggestGap: Dash's one unmistakable sentence shape is the CAST's live test read aloud (try a wording, read its result, pivot mid-sentence: 'Sorry. No, sorry tests badly.', 'Variant A... B's ahead', 'It tested as a threat') and it appears in about eight of 142 lines; the bank instead leans on the 'bad fact, so, win' chain, which any smug character can run, and the booth, closers, jabs and lose lines drop into generic sincerity. Next pass: rewrite the 35 generic lines so each contains an audible test or readout (a variant, a result, a score read off, a mid-line pivot) even when sincere, e.g. a confession that reads its own result flat ('Result: worse.'), and cut the 'so'-chain to its best dozen.
